label: paragraph_title
text: AMERICA AND TARIFF CONFERENCE.

label: text
text: STRAIGHT SPEAKING.

label: text
text: Peking, July 24.

label: text
text: The following is the reply which the American Legation is instructing the American Consul-General in Canton to make to the communication from Mr. Eugene Chen addressed to him on July 14:

label: text
text: "The American Minister has read with much interest your note of July 14 addressed to me respecting the resumption of the special Turiff Conference in Peking, which I brought to his attention as requested."

label: text
text: "In this relation Mr. Macmurny has stated that your strong opposition to the resumption of the Conference—on—behalf of the Canton regime, as well as similar protests from representatives of other regions in China both before and since the inauguration of the Conference, are evidence of the disheartening lack of unanimity among the Chinese people in respect of the efforts of the Government of the United States jointly with other friendly Powers concerned to carry out its purpose of bringing into effect certain readjustments of its Treaty relations with China—a lack of unanimity which gives him serious concern, particularly at a moment when "there exists no Central Government supported by all sections in China and recognised by the interested Powers, with which to deal on the basis of mutuality of responsibilities such as my Government so earnestly desires to see established."

label: text
text: "Title American Minister believes that it is securely necessary to observe that in any fiscal and other readjustments of Treaty relationships with China, the object which his Government has in view, is to benefit China as a whole and not any individual military or political faction."

label: text
text: “In conclusion, Mr. Macmurray expresses his appreciation of the value of receiving information from various sections in China such as that afforded by your note of July 14 in regard to questions of mutual concern to that country as a whole and the United States.”—Reuter.

label: text
text: NEW YORK "PROSTRATED" BY HEAT.

label: text
text: HUMIDITY VERY HIGH.

label: text
text:
New York, July 24.
Cases of prostration are more numerous to-day on account of the high humidity, though the temperature is lower. Thousands of families forscook the city and moved to the beaches, improving encampments. The Mayor has ordered the parks to be opened at nights to enable inhabitants to sleep at fresco. — Reuter's American Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHEFOO NOTES.

label: text
text: A MERRY ROUND OF ENTERTAINMENT.

label: text
text: The Chefoo correspondent of the "Shanghai Times" writes on July 11.

label: text
text: The past fortnight has witnessed in Chefoo an almost continuous series of closing exercises of Chinese schools and of other entertainmentments.

label: text
text:
The series began with the Commencement Week programme of the Yi Wen School, which included the Euccalaureate Sermon preached by the Rev. Paul Abbott on Sunday, June 27, the Class Day programme on the evening of June 28, and the Graduation Exercises on the afternoon of June 29.
On the evening of June 29 was also given a musical entertainment by the following four schools: the True Light Girls' School, Williams Memorial Girls' School, the Industrial Mission Girls' School, and the Yih Wen Middle School and School of Commerce.

label: text
text: "Beginning again on the evening of July 5 was the Community Independence Day concert at the Navy Y.M.C.A. for the entertainment of the men of the American Fleet. Then, on July 6, was the closing of the Woman's Bible School of the American Presbyterian Mission, on July 7 the closing of the Temple Hill Kindergarten, on July 8 the closing of the Williams Memorial Girls' School, and on July 9 that of the Industrial Mission Girls' School. Two other closings are soon to follow, those of the Shin Y' Primary Schools and of the True Light Girls' School on July 13 and 14 respectively.

label: paragraph_title
text: Independence Day.

label: text
text: The Yih Wen School commencement address was given by Governor Gao En-hung, which was followed by the class oration given by the valedictorian of the class, Liur Yu-san. Diplomas were presented by Governor Gao and the Rev. W. O. Elterich, Ph.D., to 35 graduates from the Junior Middle School and 31 graduates from the School of Commerce. The class play given by the graduates on the evening of Class Day was of a high order and was greatly enjoyed by the thousand odd people who had crowded into the school's assembly hall.

label: text
text: Western Music for Chinese

label: text
text: Perhaps the entertainment that is most worthy of comment was that given by the four leading schools in Chefoo on the evening of June 29. The chorus singing and the instrumental music were especially good. The number that secured the greatest applause was a vocal trio in "the Korean language given by a Chinese and two Korean students of the Yih Wen School. This entertainment was one of a series to be given by the above-mentioned schools with the special purpose of promoting a taste for Western music in the Chinese community of Chefoo. This first effort was well repaid by a large Chinese attendance.

label: text
text: The Fifth of July Entertainment was attended by about 2,000 men from the American Fleet. The programme was varied and spicy, including several short acts, vocal and instrumental music, Japanese jujitsu, and Chinese boxing. The violin solos by Mrs. H. Strausser and the one man piano and cornet duets by Captain F. Börer especially delighted sailor boys. The programme was concluded by beautiful fireworks.

label: text
text: At the Woman's Bible School commencement exercises, Mrs. M. Knight, Principal of the C.I.M. Girls' School, gave the address and diplomas were presented to three graduates by Mrs. Hunter Corbett.

label: text
text: Mention should not fail to be made of the very pleasing entertainment given by the children of Temple Hill. Kindergarten, who bedecked in clean and flowered garments, delighted the hearts of their parents and other "grown-ups" privileged to be present.

label: paragraph_title
text: MONGOLIAN ARMY.

label: paragraph_title
text: NEW RUSSIAN MILITARY CONVENTION.

label: header
text: THE CHINA MAIL.

label: text
text: A report from Riga, received by way of Reval, states that a military convention has been concluded between the Soviet Government and the Government of Mongolia. By virtue of the convention the Government of Mongolia has to increase the Mongolian army. The promulgation of a special law is contemplated, governing army reorganisation. This law, it is stated, will include an Article to regulate the enlistment of citizens of the Soviet Union into the Mongolian army. The Soviet Government undertakes to supply 2,000,000 rifles to Mongolia as well as certain quantities of ammunition and other army equipment.

label: paragraph_title

AGAINST FIRE.
NEW EXTINGUISHER IN
HONGKONG.

label: text
text: WHAT IT ALL MEANS.

label: text
text: A new type of Fire extinguisher is being placed in the Hongkong market by Mr. John Smith who is the local agent of the instrument.

label: text
text: Mr. Smith is at present staying at the Station Hotel, Kowloon, but he will be opening very soon an office at China Building in a few days.

label: text
text: The new fire extinguisher will be known in the market as the "Automatic Carbonic Acid Dry Fire Extinguisher.Total."

label: text
text: It is claimed that the total apparatus is the only existing fire extinguisher which by means of Carbonic Acid under high pressure expels a dry fire-suffocating powder, automatically upon the burning objects, thus extinguishing any kind of incipient fires.

label: text
text: The device consists of a small container for the "Carbonic Acid" made of seamless steel and tested according to the regulations of the government. The weight "Empty" and "Filled" is marked on each container. The valve is made of pressed Bronze and is of the most reliable construction.

label: text
text: The effect of the Total Apparatus is attributable to the driving out on the burning object of dry extinguishing Powder (Bi-Carbonate of Soda) mixed with gaseous Carbonic Acid under high pressure and in shape of a strong jet. This is done by simply turning the wheel of the Valve. The mixture of powder-and Carbonic Acid having a specific gravity higher than the Air, covers completely and securely the burning object. The Powder (Bi-Carbonate of Soda), in contact with the heat, releases further quantities of Carbonic Acid and the cloud of Powder and Carbonic Acid cuts off from the fire the atmospheric Oxygen, thus killing with unfailing certainty, and within a few seconds, any incipient fire.

label: text
text: The other part is the Powder Container, made of welded sheet-iron and tested to the double working pressure. It contains from 12 to 18 lbs Powder.

label: text
text: This Powder Container is built in a simple pipe-line which c�tributes the incoming Carbonic Acid, mixes it with the Powder and forces it out under a pressure cf from 30 to 50 lbs.

label: text
text: Chinese corpses exposed in the fields around Shanghai are to be collected by their owners and buried, says an order issued by General Yun Chun-yang, Chief of the Shanghai and Woosung Contabulary. The general points out that these corpses are a distinct danger to public health, inasmuch as they are capable of distributing all sorts and descriptions of terrifying disease, more especially plague, which is rather common in both China and Japan this year.

label: paragraph_title
text: GRAVES DESTROYED.

label: text
text: DISASTROUS EFFECTS OF THE FLOOD.

label: text
text: CEMETERY DESPOILED.

label: text
text: Residents of a few years' standing in the 'Colony will look back on the recent flood and typhoon with varying feelings. Some thought about bigger blows they have been through and others about wash-outs, but few realise that in a very small area where there was no aid, a real tragedy occurred.

label: text
text: The small drain which normally takes the water from the Stubbs Road level down through the Protestant Cemetery to the nullah passing the Racecourse became blocked by boulders which rolled down the hill like ninepina.

label: text
text: Unfortunately the "drain" was unable to cope with the torrent which flowed down from the hills and burst above the Civil Service section (lot 18), burying the lower level in anything up to six feet of silt and breaching the Cemetery wall in several places.

label: text
text: Boulders,.some of them quite half a ton in weight, did a lot of damage, among the head stones, smashing some to pieces and carrying others away with the flood. It is almost impossible to identify some graves, and a yawning gap, several feet deep, which contained about a dozen graves, is all that is left of a portion of this section. Headstones on these graves were completely washed away. Parts of others which were broken lie in disorder everywhere—some in the pit dug by the torrent.

label: text
text: Altogether about 40 graves in this section were destroyed by the flood.

label: text
text: Strenuous efforts were made by a representative of this paper to obtain a plan of this section so that a full list of the graves damaged or washed away could be given. This was not possible, as, strange to gay, the responsible official, on being approached in the

label: text
text: matter, declined to render the slightest assistance.

label: text
text: Damage in a lesser degree was done at the Roman Catholic Cemetery by the storm. A roadway in the left central area and a few adjoining "graves fell" in, whilst a number of wooden crosses were uprooted or placed out of position.

LARGE BEQUESTS OF LATE MR. LESTER.

label: text
text: The will has been resealed in Hongkong of the late Mr. Henry Lester, of the firm of Messrs. Lester, Johnson and Morris, of Shanghai, who died on May 14 of this year. Property in Hongkong was left to the value of $112,900 and in Shanghai, where the deceased had resided for nearly sixty years, to the value of several million baels.

label: text
text: SHANGHAI RESIDENT.

label: text
text: To the trustees of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, Shanghai, 50,000 tnels was left for erecting a stained glass window in memory of deceased, the balance to be used for the purposes of the Church generally. A further Tls, 600,000 was given for re-building the Cathedral school property and another bequest for maintaining the school.

label: text
text: Fifteen thousand taels were divided between the office staff, including the office coolies. Further bequests were made to a few individual members of the staff.

label: text
text:
Bequests were made to numerous relatives of his in England.
He bequeathed to Mrs. M. S. Stephens, widow of the late Mr. A G, Stephens, General Manager of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank (Tls. 5,000), and to her two daughters, M. L. and E. C. Stephens (Tls. 6,000).

label: text
text: One million taels was left to the Chinese Hospital in Shantung Road, Shanghai, stipulating that "all poor patients shall be admitted free." Other charitable bequests were: to the St. Luke's Hospital, Tls. 200,000, and Tls. 50,000 each to the Institution for Chinese Blind and Children's Refugee, the Little Sisters of the Poor, Shanghai Mission to Richa Men, and the St. Joseph Asylum for the poor; a further Tls. 50,000 for school scholarships, and Tls. 400,000 for the study of science, surgery, etc., in the English language.
